In brief

Parody. "Mr Cowe Conacre (Multifarnham. Nat.): Arising out of the question of my honourable friend, the member for Shillelagh, may I ask the right honourable gentleman […] (The house rises. Cheers.)": parodying debate in the British House of Commons, a new kind of stylistic extravagance comments on the news that Joseph Nannetti is traveling to London to address the question of how to control the spread of "foot and mouth disease" in cattle, and also the unrelated issue of "forbidding Irish games in the park." Like the parodic account of the conversation between Bloom and Dennis Breen, this dialogue presents raw reality in elegantly distanced language. The boiling nationalist passions of the men in the pub are expressed with the stylized formality of a parliamentary proceeding, where even bitter enemies address one another as "the right honourable gentleman."

At more length

Joe Hynes has been telling the Citizen that he saw Nannetti talking about FMD with another MP at a meeting of cattle traders. The two, he says, "are going over tonight to London to ask about it on the floor of the house of commons." Gifford infers that the talk will be about whether to slaughter and bury every animal in infected herds or quarantine herds but kill only the infected animals.

Hynes adds that a nationalist sports organization has asked Nannetti also to complain that the commissioner of the DMP has ruled that Gaelic games cannot be played in Phoenix Park, even though English games are allowed: "The league told him to ask a question tomorrow about the commissioner of police forbidding Irish games in the park. What do you think of that, citizen? The Sluagh na h-Eireann." This nationalist organization, whose name means "Host (Army) of Ireland," did ask Nannetti to raise the question, but Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note that the question was asked on 30 June 1904 by a different MP traveling with him, Thomas O'Donnell: "I beg to ask the Chief Secretary to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland [...] why the members of Sluagh na Heirann, most of whom are school boys, are prevented from playing native games in the Nine Acres."

Both issues are charged with emotion for Irishmen, and the debate begins with one Nationalist ("Nat.") MP seconding another's question "whether the government has issued orders that these animals shall be slaughtered though no medical evidence is forthcoming as to their pathological condition?" The MPs are fictional. "Multifarnham" is an actual village northwest of Mullingar in County Westmeath, deep in cattle country, and the county did have two National Party MPs at the time, but neither was named "Cowe Conacre" and neither was from that town. The name evokes the Conacre ("corn acres") System by which wealthy 19th century landowners rented small plots of their land to half-starving peasant farmers at punishing rates. Mr. Conacre refers to "my honourable friend, the member for Shillelagh." Shillelagh too was an actual village in County Wicklow, and this county likewise had two MPs, but neither seat was attached specifically to Shillelagh. It enters the text because, as Gifford observes, "Shillelagh is famous for its oak trees; hence the use of its name for the Irish cudgel." These two members, then, metaphorically stand for Irish Catholic poverty, pride, resentment, and nationalist resistance.

The representative of His Majesty's government to whom Conacre addresses his question is "Mr Allfours (Tamoshant. Con.)," and here once more Joyce paints with broad brushstrokes. The British Prime Minister in 1904, a Conservative ("Con."), was Arthur James Balfour. Balfour was Scottish, a fact that Joyce playfully foregrounds by substituting the name of the national cap (tam o'shanter) for the district which the honorable member represents. Earlier in his career (1887-91), Balfour had served in the Conservative cabinet as Chief Secretary for Ireland. Gifford notes that because of his enforcement of the government "policy of 'coercion' (instant and severe police measures against any expression of Irish Nationalist sentiment), he earned among the Irish the nickname Bloody Balfour." The Countess of Fingall writes that "I don't think he ever liked the Irish or understood them" (210). Mr. Allfours, then (a man "all for" fighting? a beast crawling on "all fours"?), has little respect for challenges from Irish nationalists and he responds to Mr. Conacre's question with curt dismissive contempt: "I feel I cannot usefully add anything to that. The answer to the honourable member's question is in the affirmative."

The brusque rejection of one Irish complaint triggers another as a second National Party MP rises to question the PM: "Mr Orelli O'Reilly (Montenotte. Nat.): Have similar orders been issued for the slaughter of human animals who dare to play Irish games in the Phoenix park?" Mr. Balfour's reply to this brutal sarcasm is terser still: "The answer is in the negative." Montenotte is a suburb of Cork and Cork was represented by nine Nationalist MPs, but none was named O'Reilly. Joyce's invention enables him to produce a member whose first name is a homophone of his last. O'Reilly rises to say "Oh really?" to Bloody Balfour's plan to exterminate whole herds of Irish cattle, asking whether his bloodlust extends to exterminating "human animals" who play rough native games like hurling rather than genteel English games like cricket and polo.

Partisan rancor rises to fever pitch when Mr. Conacre stirs up bitter memories of events nearly two decades earlier: "Has the right honourable gentleman's famous Mitchelstown telegram inspired the policy of gentlemen on the Treasury bench?" In 1904 Balfour was the Treasury secretary as well as Prime Minister. In 1887, as Chief Secretary for Ireland, he supported the Cabinet's policy of violent "coercion." On September 9 of that year a Land League meeting in the New Square of Mitchelstown, in County Cork, had drawn about 8,000 people to protest the prosecution of two local Nationalist MPs who had helped organize rent strikes on the nearby Kingston estate. As several policemen tried to push through the crowd to take incriminating notes on the speeches being given at the front, pushing and shoving ensued, then hand-to-hand combat, and finally rifle fire from a nearby barracks. Three men died.

There was angry opposition in Parliament, which William Gladstone and Irish MPs later stoked with the phrase "Remember Mitchelstown!" Balfour, challenged in the House, could only lamely read from a short telegram summarizing the police's version of events. Mr. Conacre asks whether that honourable gentleman now justifies slaughtering Irish cattle on the same grounds as he once defended the slaughter of Irish men. Mr. Allfours responds with a parliamentary dodge: "I must have notice of that question." A Prime Minister addressing the House may refuse to reply to a question if the topic has not been previously introduced into debate. The member who wishes to raise it must then submit a formal request to bring it to the floor, giving the minister time to prepare a response.

Allfours's reiterated cowardice draws jeers from the opposition, beginning with a taunt from an Independent MP: "Mr Staylewit (Buncombe. Ind.): Don't hesitate to shoot." The 18th century-sounding "Staylewit" requires no gloss, but "buncombe," meaning windy irrelevant speechmaking, comes from an episode in the US House of Representatives when Felix Walker, representing Buncombe County in western North Carolina, could not be dissuaded from speaking. The people of his district expected it, he said, so he was duty-bound to "make a speech for Buncombe." Mr. Staylewit's contribution to the debate is to parrot the words of the commander of the police barracks in Mitchelstown: "Don't hesitate to shoot if necessary." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner, citing a 1904 English translation of Émile Boutmy's The English People: A Study of their Political Psychology, note that "a telegram with this command was read to the British parliament where it was met with 'indecent joy'."

Mr. Allfours has no wish to be drawn into discussion of embarrassing telegrams, but the House erupts in loud cheers and jeers from the opposition. The dialogue in this parodic passage does not correspond to any dialogue happening in the pub, but it surely conveys the feelings of the men there.

John Hunt 2026
